archetype.name: Cup Contender (offense-first, goaltending in question)
archetype.definition: A team that controls play and scores near the top of the league, as it did in last year's league-best season, but whose ceiling now depends on whether its goaltending returns to anything like last year's level.

report.headline: Elite offense and real play-driving, propped up by finishing and failed by goaltending
report.take:
Colorado is coming off a 121-point season in which it ranked first on the site, first in offense and first in defense. The early version of 2026-27 looks like the same team in most ways. The Avalanche score 4.22 goals a game, second in the league. They put 30.8 shots on goal a night, fourth in the league, and own 56.1% of the 5-on-5 expected goals, fifth best. The skaters grade out as a top group: forwards A-, blueline A. Nathan MacKinnon has 16 points and 38 shots, and Cale Makar sits second on the defensemen tab. Their pace is 51 wins and 113 points, which already sits behind last year's level.

The gap is in net, and it is the biggest change from last year. Last season's goalies saved 34.3 goals above expected. This year's are at -2.7, 23rd in the league, and the goaltending grade is a C-. Mackenzie Blackwood has taken six of the starts at a .891 save percentage and -2.1 GSAx, so the starter is the one leaking. The team's all-situations save percentage of .894 is basically league average, but the shots it faces have been better than that number suggests. That is why a club allowing 25.9 shots a game still ranks only 11th in goals allowed a game.

The numbers hide how much finishing is doing for the offense. Colorado shoots 14.6% in all situations, third in the league, against a league mark of 11.3%. Its 5-on-5 PDO is 106.8, and that shooting is the main reason. Some of it is individual: Artturi Lehkonen has six goals on 12 shots, while Nazem Kadri has none on 24. Over the last five games the shooting cooled and the scoring fell to 3.0 a game. The result was a 2-2-1 stretch with a -1 differential, a preview of what happens when the finishing normalizes and the goaltending doesn't improve.

The underlying play is the part that lasts. A 56% expected-goals share and a top-ten penalty kill at 85% are the bones of a contender, and the -1 Pts vs Goal Diff says the record is slightly behind the margin rather than ahead of it. Expect the goal rate to drift down toward the high 3s. Whether this ends as a 100-point team or a 115-point team comes down to the crease.

strengths.title: Controls 5-on-5 play
strengths.body: Colorado owns 56.1% of the 5-on-5 expected goals, fifth in the league and well above the even-split mark. That matches last year's 56.9%, so the possession game is a carried-over identity, not an October fluke. It rests on a deep center group: MacKinnon and Martin Necas both drive over 60% of the expected goals when they're on the ice.

strengths.title: MacKinnon and Makar at full power
strengths.body: MacKinnon has 16 points and 38 shots and leads the team in Game Score by a wide margin. Makar ranks second among all defensemen on the site with nine points. A shot volume like MacKinnon's is repeatable even when his finishing cools. Two players of this level make an A-grade skater group sturdy.

strengths.title: A penalty kill that travels
strengths.body: The kill is at 85%, eighth in the league and six points above the league average. Last year's group killed 84.6%, so this is a stable skill rather than a hot start. It also helps cover for goaltending that isn't stealing anything at even strength.

concerns.title: Goaltending has fallen off a cliff
concerns.body: Team GSAx sits at -2.7, 23rd in the league, a stark drop from last season's 34.3. Blackwood carries most of the starts at .891 with -2.1 GSAx, and Scott Wedgewood hasn't been much better. Eight games is too small a sample to call it permanent. But this is the one group grading poorly, and it caps everything else.

concerns.title: Shooting luck inflating the goal rate
concerns.body: A 14.6% team shooting percentage, third in the league, is far above the league's 11.3%. Combined with a 106.8 PDO at 5-on-5, it means the scoring rate is running hot. Lehkonen's six goals on 12 shots won't hold. The last five games already showed the regression, with scoring falling to 3.0 a game.

concerns.title: Opposing defensemen get loose
concerns.body: Colorado allows 2.13 points a game to opposing defensemen, 0.43 above what those players usually produce, 26th in the league. Defensemen account for 28.3% of the points scored against Colorado, versus 24.2% league-wide. That points to point shots and pinches getting through. Better goaltending would hide some of it.

trend.note: A blowout start of 8-4 and 6-1 has given way to alternating wins and losses. The last five went 2-2-1 with a -1 differential as the shooting cooled and the goaltending stayed flat.

weekAhead.headline: Two elite possession teams, then a soft Nashville finish
weekAhead.body:
The week opens the night after a loss in Philadelphia, with a road game in New Jersey. The Devils are the league's best possession team, first in xGF % and CF %, with 35 shots a game. But their goalies have been the worst part of their season: .869 save percentage, -4.7 GSAx, and a 69.6% penalty kill, 27th. For Colorado's shooters that is the most generous net on the schedule. For Blackwood or Wedgewood it is the heaviest shot volume they'll see. It sets up as a track meet.

Tampa Bay at home is the real test. The Lightning are second in xGF %, allow only 22.8 shots a game and hold opposing forwards well under their norms. Their 6-2-0 record leans on close-game luck, though, with Pts vs Goal Diff third in the league. Their power play is 30th. The week closes in Nashville against a team that gets outshot at 5-on-5 but has B+ goaltending and a power play converting 29.6%. Colorado should drive play there; the question is whether it can solve a hot goalie.

keyMatchups.title: Makar and Toews versus New Jersey
keyMatchups.body: New Jersey allows opposing defensemen 3.13 points a game, 1.53 above expectation, the worst mark in the league. Centers also feast there, at 0.78 over expected, 28th. Combine that with the Devils' shaky goaltending and this is the spot for Colorado's blueline and MacKinnon to fill the sheet.

keyMatchups.title: Tampa's lockdown on wingers
keyMatchups.body: Tampa holds opposing wingers a full point a game below their norms, fifth in the league, and forwards overall rank sixth. Lehkonen and Gabriel Landeskog will find it hard going, which puts the burden on the centers. Colorado's edge is special teams: Tampa's power play converts just 10.7% against Colorado's top-ten kill.

keyMatchups.title: Nashville's goalie and power play
keyMatchups.body: The Predators control only 44% of the 5-on-5 shot attempts, 27th, so Colorado should own the puck. Their goalies sit ninth in GSAx, and their power play converts 29.6%, fourth. Discipline and finishing decide this one, not territory.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Colorado's goalies can hold up against New Jersey's 35 shots a night on the second half of a back-to-back.

restOfSeason.body:
The 5-on-5 control, the depth down the middle and the penalty kill are all sustainable. They match last year's profile, when Colorado was the site's top team. The 14.6% shooting and 106.8 PDO are not sustainable. Expect the goal rate to slide from 4.22 a game into the 3.4-3.8 range as Lehkonen and Necas cool, partly offset if Kadri's zero-goal start on 24 shots turns around.

The swing piece is goaltending. If Blackwood settles into a league-average save percentage, the play-driving alone should carry this team to the 104-114 point range and a top seed in the Central. If the goaltending stays below expected all year, the cooling offense will expose it, and they look more like a 100-point team that bleeds close games.

confidence.note: Eight to nine games is a thin sample, but the possession profile matches multiple prior seasons.
